{{Short description|American scientist (1936–2025)}}
'''Roland Winston''' (February 12, 1936 – February 8, 2025) was an American scientist who was a leading figure in the field of [[nonimaging optics]]<ref name="IntroNio2e">{{cite book | first = Julio | last = Chaves | title = Introduction to Nonimaging Optics, Second Edition |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=e11ECgAAQBAJ | publisher = [[CRC Press]] |  year = 2015 | isbn = 978-1-4822-0673-9}}</ref> and its applications to solar energy, and is sometimes termed the "father of non-imaging optics".<ref name="opn"/><ref name="emil"/> He was the inventor of the [[Nonimaging optics#Compound parabolic concentrator|compound parabolic concentrator]] (CPC), a breakthrough technology in solar energy. He was also a former Guggenheim Fellow, past head of the University of Chicago Department of Physics, a member of the founding faculty of [[University of California Merced]]. He was nominated as head of the California Advanced Solar Technologies Institute in 2013.<ref name="poly"/>

Winston held more than 25 patents,<ref name="emil">{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ia2JOmU4BvMC&pg=PA167|page=167|title=Tribute To Emil Wolf: Science And Engineering Legacy Of Physical Optics|isbn=0-8194-5441-9|last1=Wolf|first1=Emil|last2=Jannson|first2=Tomasz P.|year=2005|publisher=SPIE Press }}</ref> chiefly related to solar energy, and has been figuratively said to have a "patent on the sun".<ref name="sunpatent">{{Cite news|url=http://chronicle.uchicago.edu/040415/winston.shtml|author=Steve Koppes|date=2004-04-15|access-date=2013-05-28|title=Winston's research leads to 'patent on the sun' for solar energy development |work=University of Chicago Chronicle}}</ref>
[[File:Roland Winston Shimer College 1952.jpg|thumb|Roland Winston in 1952.]]

==Background==
Roland Winston was born in [[Moscow|Moscow, Russia]] to Claudia Goretskaya, a Russian chemical engineer and to Joseph Winston, an American engineer who helped Russians design towns and build an industrial base.  At the beginning of [[World War II]],  after the signing of the [[Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact|Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact]], Roland's father was expelled from the USSR, leaving his wife and son behind. In 1943, young Roland and his mother, that had been evacuated to Kuibyshev (now Samara), managed to leave the USSR with the help of American authorities and US Air Force long-range bombers.

In the USA, Winston first attended the [[Bronx High School of Science]]<ref name="Early life">{{cite web |url=https://news.ucmerced.edu/news/2022/retiring-winston-looks-forward-his-busy-bright-future|title=Growing Up|date=2022-06-13|access-date=2022-06-13}}</ref> and then enrolled as an early entrant at [[Shimer College]] in 1950, transferring to the [[University of Chicago]] after two years.<ref name="convocation">{{Cite news|title=Shimer College Convocation For Graduates Set Sunday|author=Consolidated News Service|page=B1|work=Rockford Register-Republic|date=1953-05-27}}</ref><ref name="founding"/>  He received a BA from Shimer in 1953, in a graduating class of 11, including future cosmologist [[Jerome Kristian]].<ref name="convocation"/>  Continuing with advanced undergraduate study at the University of Chicago, he received a BS in 1956.<ref name="profile"/>

Winston remained at [[University of Chicago]] for his graduate work in physics, completing his MS in 1957 and his Ph.D. in 1963.<ref name="profile">{{Cite web|url=http://engineering.ucmerced.edu/content/roland-winston|title=Roland Winston|publisher=UC Merced School of Engineering|access-date=2013-05-29}}</ref>  He studied under figures including [[Yoichiro Nambu]] and [[Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar]].<ref name="opn"/>  Winston's doctoral dissertation was on "observable hyperfine effects in [[muon capture]] by complex nuclei."<ref>{{Cite web |website=Worldcat |title=Observable hyperfine effects in muon capture by complex nuclei |url=https://www.worldcat.org/title/49434477 |oclc=49434477}}</ref>

Winston died on February 8, 2025, at the age of 88.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Anderson |first1=Lorena |title=Founding Faculty Roland Winston Remembered for Pioneering Solar Energy |url=https://news.ucmerced.edu/news/2025/founding-faculty-roland-winston-remembered-pioneering-solar-energy |access-date=20 February 2025 |publisher=UC Merced |date=18 February 2025}}</ref>

==Scientific career==
Winston initially developed the underlying concept of the CPC for use in the study of [[Cherenkov radiation]] while working at [[Argonne National Laboratory]] in 1966.<ref name="opn">{{Cite news |date=April 2009 |title=2009 OSA Awards |page= |work=OSA News Release |url=https://www.optica.org/about/newsroom/news_releases/2009/the_optical_society_bestows_17_awards_for_2009/ |access-date=2023-12-09}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|work=State Times Advocate|title=Energy Solution Seen in Research|page=8|date=1974-06-16|author=UPI}}</ref>  He was prompted to invent the CPC several years later in 1974, when Argonne director [[Robert Sachs]] asked him if it would be possible to extend the parabolic approach to solar energy applications, and if so, whether it would be superior to the existing systems that used imaging optics.<ref name="schertz">{{Cite book|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=6LPdXPzw1JsC&pg=PA747|title=Implementation of Solar Thermal Technology|chapter=Argonne National Laboratory|author=William W. Schertz|page=747|year=1996|publisher=MIT Press |isbn=0-262-12187-5}}</ref>  Only a year after the invention of the CPC, it was discovered that this design had been anticipated by hundreds of millions of years by the eyes of the [[horseshoe crab]].{{sfn|Gilmore|1976|p=168}} The paper announcing this discovery was also coauthored by Winston.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=The corneal cones of Limulus as optimised light concentrators|author1=R. Levi-Setti |author2=D.A. Park |author3=R. Winston |journal=Nature|date=1975-01-10|pages=115–116|volume=253|issue=5487|doi=10.1038/253115a0|pmid=1110755|bibcode=1975Natur.253..115L|s2cid=4207913}}</ref>

A key advantage of the CPC over the earlier imaging collectors was that it could achieve very high efficiencies without needing to track the sun.<ref>{{Cite news|work=Popular Science|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=CgEAAAAAMBAJ&pg=PA50|page=50|author=Arthur Fisher|title=Solar Concentrator|date=June 1976}}</ref>  Non-tracking collectors had previously been believed to be impossible to design.<ref name="opn"/>  In addition, CPCs received considerable media attention for their ability to function even under heavily clouded and hazy skies.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Solar collector works on hazy days|agency=Associated Press|date=1974-05-20|page=4}}</ref>

Winston and Joseph O'Gallagher devised a more refined version of the CPC in 1982, which was smaller and eliminated the need for an extra layer of glass.<ref>{{Cite news|work=Popular Science|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=q0qVc8dQrpgC&pg=PA30|page=30|date=July 1982|title=Concentrating collector yields high heat without tracking the sun|author=Robert Anderson}}</ref>

In 1988, using a new mirror-based technique, Winston and his team set a new record for concentration of solar energy, concentrating sunlight to more than 60,000 times its normal intensity.<ref>{{Cite news|work=New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1988/03/11/us/scientists-using-mirrors-match-energy-intensity-of-sun-s-surface.html|author=John Noble Wilford|title=Scientists, Using Mirrors, Match Energy Intensity of Sun's Surface|date=1988-03-11|access-date=2013-05-29}}</ref>  In 1989, Winston coauthored with W.T. Welford what became the defining text of the field, ''High Collection Nonimaging Optics''.  Later revised under the name of ''Nonimaging Optics'', it remains a classic in the field.

From 1989 to 1995, he served as chair of the Department of Physics of the University of Chicago.<ref name="poly">{{Cite web|url=http://www.polyu.edu.hk/feng/icnp_aom2013/uploads/Bio_RolandWinston.pdf|title=Roland Winston|publisher=Hong Kong Polytechnic University|access-date=2013-05-29}}</ref> In addition to his solar energy work, he has continued to work in his original field of high-energy physics, conducting experiments at Argonne and [[Fermilab]].<ref name="poly"/>{{sfn|Shrum et al.|2007|p=44}}

In 2003, Winston left the University of Chicago, where he had been working and studying since 1952, to join the founding faculty of the University of California Merced.<ref name="founding">{{cite web|url=http://www.ucmerced.edu/news/uc-merced-appoints-first-founding-faculty|title=UC Merced Appoints First Founding Faculty|date=2003-03-17|access-date=2013-05-29}}</ref> He has however remained connected the U of C and the city of Chicago, and has remained affiliated with the university's [[Enrico Fermi Institute]].<ref name="sunpatent"/> In 2004 he partnered with Chicago company [[Solargenix Energy]] to create roof-integrated solar cooling and heating systems.<ref name="sunpatent"/>

On June 13, 2022, Winston announced he would retire on July 1. Of the first eight founding faculty members, he was the first one to leave after nearly two decades of service to the UC Merced and the University of California system.<ref name="retires">{{cite web |url=https://news.ucmerced.edu/news/2022/retiring-winston-looks-forward-his-busy-bright-future|title=Distinguished Professor Retires|date=2022-06-13|access-date=2022-06-13}}</ref>

==Awards and recognition==
Winston has received numerous awards in the course of his career, including a [[Guggenheim Fellowship]] in 1977<ref>http://www.gf.org/fellows/15941-roland-winston {{Dead link|date=February 2022}}</ref> and the Joseph Fraunhofer Award for "significant accomplishments in optical engineering" from the Optical Society of America in 2009.<ref name="opn"/>  He was elected as a US delegate to the [[International Solar Energy Society]] in 1991.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Solar Today|volume=5|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Xi1QAAAAYAAJ|page=7|year=1991}}</ref> Also in 1991, he was elected a Fellow of OSA.

Devices to which Winston's name has become attached include the CPC itself, which is sometimes known as a "Winston solar collector",<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=9sOd56DqLFkC&pg=PA564|page=564|title=Dictionary of Energy: Expanded Edition|editor1=Cutler J. Cleveland |editor2=Christopher G. Morris|year=2009|isbn=978-0-08-096517-8|last1=Cleveland|first1=Cutler J.|last2=Morris|first2=Christopher G.|publisher=Elsevier }}</ref> and "[[Winston cone]]s", the individual parabolic elements that make up a CPC.
